item.title: Long Rest Ends at Hour 7: Party Slept in Giant Badger's Den
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: Friends, the Soft Landing Company took a long rest in a cozy root cellar near Gorsewick. A giant badger was hibernating in it. At hour seven, it woke.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, five adventurers from the Soft Landing Company bedded down for a long rest on Thursday night in a root cellar under an empty farmstead outside Gorsewick, and a giant badger was already asleep in it. It was hibernating under a heap of straw in the back corner. At hour seven of eight, it woke up.

The party came to my clinic Friday morning with fourteen claw scratches between them, one bedroll chewed clean through, and a fighter wearing a single boot. Nobody got their spells back. "We had one hour to go," said Oswin Harle, the party's wizard, while I cleaned his ear. "One. I could feel the slots coming back. Then my pillow growled."

Here is what happened, as near as I can piece it together. The cellar was warm and dry and smelled of earth and stored turnips, which is what a badger looks for in a bedroom too. The party's cleric, Brin Calloway, admits she saw "a big furry lump" in the corner and took it for a pile of old coats. Around hour five the wizard ran out of floor and put his head on it. Around hour seven the bard began to snore in a key the lump did not care for.

Now, the science. The old herbals say never wake a sleeping badger, and they say it kindly. The naturalists at Candlekeep put it in plainer numbers: a badger doesn't sleep the whole winter straight through. It drops into a deep torpor, heart slowed, body cooled, living off its autumn fat. Waking up is the expensive part. Warming back up burns a good deal of that stored fat, so every time somebody rouses it in late November, it spends a piece of its winter pantry.

So yes, I patched the party, and I'm on the badger's side. Five strangers moved into its bedroom and one used it as a pillow. It chased them up the ladder, ate the bedroll, kept the boot, and went back to sleep, which is more restraint than I'd show. Gorsewick's farm warden has since left a basket of earthworms and windfall pears by the cellar door and nailed up a sign reading OCCUPIED UNTIL SPRING. Before anyone writes in: this was not the Thornbury Irregulars' fighter who came back from the Reincarnate rite as a badger. He keeps a room in town and gets up at a reasonable hour.

My advice for anyone planning a long rest in the wild is simple. Check the corners before you lie down. Poke any heap with a ten-foot pole, and stand at the far end of it. If a spot is suspiciously cozy, something else probably found it first. My friend Nyx Spindlecoil tells me there's a charm now that buzzes when a den is occupied. Go outside, Nyx, and look in the den.

For the Soft Landing Company I prescribe a pot of chestnut-and-parsnip soup and a proper eight hours at an inn with a door that locks. For the badger, I prescribe quiet.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Bugbear Wins Pie-Eating Contest, Then Eats the Table
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: A bugbear fighter won Fish Street's pie-eating contest and its 20 gp purse for his broke party. Then he allegedly ate the 32 gp table.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell after noon, a bugbear fighter named Grukka Mossjaw allegedly won the Fish Street pie-eating contest outside the Brass Kettle bakery, finishing 41 pies in six minutes to take the 20 gp prize purse. He then ate the table, which was oak. The bakery has billed his adventuring party, the Thin Purse Company, 32 gold pieces for it, which leaves the party 12 gold in the hole on a contest it won.

The Thin Purse Company entered for the money. According to the party's wizard and treasurer, Elsbeth Rook, the group's whole treasury before the contest was three copper pieces, a button, and an IOU from a goblin. "We had a plan," Rook said, holding the ledger. "The plan was pie. Nobody put a line in the plan about furniture."

Netterly and two fishwives say Mossjaw cleared his last pie with a minute to spare, raised both arms, and was handed the purse. Then, allegedly, he leaned down and bit the corner off the judging table. "I thought he was checking it for crumbs," said Hob Netterly, a cooper who was holding a pie of his own at the time. "Then the whole leg went. He chewed it like a carrot. I put my pie down. I didn't want it anymore."

The bakery's owner, Wilda Oatley, says the table had stood outside the Brass Kettle for nineteen years. "My grandmother rolled crusts on that table," she said. "He ate the part she rolled them on." Oatley also says the bugbear ate the tablecloth, two pie tins, and the little brass judge's bell, which was very shiny and which I would like to state for the record I saw first. It had a lovely ring to it. Anyway.

The City Watch arrived at roughly the third bell and allegedly found a bugbear asleep on the cobbles beside four table legs, three of them bitten. A Watch sergeant took statements and confiscated nothing, because there was nothing left to confiscate. A pigeon tried to take the last crust. I chased it off. You're welcome, Fish Street.

The party's cleric, a dwarf named Tobber Greystave, reportedly argued that the table was "part of the presentation" and therefore part of the contest. Oatley disagreed. So did the rulebook, which is one page long and says "pies" eleven times. It was nailed to the table. Mossjaw ate it, so nobody can check.

Rook paid the bakery the 20 gp purse on the spot and signed for the remaining 12 against the party's next dungeon. Oatley says she'll take it in coin or in a new table, built to the old size. "And he stays on the far side of it," she added. It's been a bad week for Brindlemoor pies, what with kobolds carried off 120 of them from windowsills on the 22nd.

Reached in the Brass Kettle's alley, where he was allegedly sleeping it off, Mossjaw gave a short statement. "Good table," he said. "Bit dry." The bakery says next year's contest will be held on the ground.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Umber Hulk Tunnel Dodges 3-Copper Toll, Links Two Baronies
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: An adventuring party paid an umber hulk 40 gold to dodge a 3-copper bridge toll. Smugglers found the tunnel first. Both baronies want the party.
item.content:encoded:
An adventuring party hired an umber hulk to dig a tunnel under the river rather than pay the three-copper toll at Quillmarch Bridge. The tunnel came up in Brackwater. Smugglers found it four days before the customs house did, and now Ashenfold and Brackwater agree on exactly one thing: it is the party's fault. Tension holds at fourteen siege-days.

The party is the Sallowmoss Company. Four adventurers, one mule. The toll is three copper a head, up from two since the troll's toll hike last month. The mule counts as a head. Total owed: fifteen copper. The umber hulk charged forty gold.

"We did the arithmetic," said Bresk Hollin, the company's wizard. "We did it afterward. Most of our arithmetic happens afterward."

The contract said to dig until daylight. The umber hulk dug for one night, came up in the root cellar of a Brackwater cooper, and kept the forty gold. The company walked through, saved fifteen copper, and went on to their quest. Nobody filled in the hole. Nobody told anyone about the hole. This is how wars start, and also how cheese gets cheaper.

By the fourth day, somebody had hung a lantern at the Ashenfold end and a sign reading TUNNEL, 2 COPPER. Untaxed Ashenfold cheese was moving north by the cartload. Brackwater pickled eels were moving south. The smugglers undercut the bridge by one copper and threw in shelter from the rain. Customs found the tunnel on the fifth day, when an inspector followed the smell of eels.

Gorvash Pennyfist, troll of Quillmarch Bridge for nine winters, took it hard. "They stole my trade. Under my own river," he said. "Now goat prices will go up. They always do." He did not explain the goats. I did not ask.

The two baronies held an emergency parley at the midpoint of the tunnel, under the river, in the dark. Envoy Halric Dunmere of Ashenfold shook hands with Envoy Teodra Hallowmere of Brackwater. Firm, two seconds, no hidden dagger detected, although nobody could see. Dunmere said the tunnel opens into Brackwater, so it is a Brackwater tunnel. Hallowmere said the tunnel starts in Ashenfold, so it is an Ashenfold export, and she will tariff it by the foot. They talked for three hours. A cart of cheese went by twice.

Both baronies have now posted writs for the Sallowmoss Company: Ashenfold for smuggling, Brackwater for unlicensed digging. The company is reported to be hiding in the tunnel itself. It is the only ground in the region neither side has claimed. They are paying the smugglers two copper a night to stay.

I went down to see it. Damp. Low ceiling. Good footing. I ate field rations at the midpoint and they tasted the same as above ground, which is the point of field rations. Ottoline Vex covered the parley from a balcony in Brindlemoor. The balcony has no tunnel. Her readers should know that.

Gorvash says the toll is four copper now, effective immediately, to cover losses. Hollin says next time the company will pay. Nobody believes either of them.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: Halfling Cooks Strike Before Feast, Led by Organizer's Cousins
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: All 38 halfling cooks walked off Brindlemoor's Grand Feast two days out. Eleven are the Feastwarden's cousins. Their offered pay was a first helping.
item.content:encoded:
The halfling cooks walked out.

All 38 cooks of the Hearthside Cooks' Guild put down their ladles Tuesday morning, two days before Brindlemoor's Grand Feast. The feast committee has 900 gp and has promised to feed 2,000 people on the Town Green on the 26th. Eleven of the strikers are cousins of the man who made that promise, Feastwarden Odo Plumbrook.

The committee's pay offer was "the honor of the first helping." That means no wages. It means you cook for 2,000 people for three days and then you get to eat some of it before they do.

"I've cooked for weddings, wakes and one siege," said Tansy Plumbrook, head pastry cook and the Feastwarden's first cousin on his mother's side. "Nobody ever paid me in soup I made myself."

The guild wants two silver a cook a day and a half-hour lunch break, sitting down, in a chair. That's the whole list. I'd sign that in my own blood. I'd sign it in Plumbrook's.

So where did the 900 gp go? Ask the kitchen, which got none of it. The committee spent 591 gp on a griffon egg named Gilbert, who has not hatched and has not peeled a potato. It pays rent on a stall at the Sleeping Mule for Duchess the boar and her nine piglets. The potatoes got peeled by an adventuring party paid in exposure. I covered that. I'm still angry about it.

Plumbrook answered from a chair on the Green. "A strong start!" he said. "This is the fun part." Fun for whom, he didn't say. He has bought three scrolls of unseen servant from a hedge wizard on Tanner's Row and says the invisible helpers will do the stirring.

The hedge wizard, Fenwick Starle, would like that on record as Plumbrook's idea. "They'll stir all night. They can't taste," he said. "Last one I lent out salted a custard until it was a rock. The customer used it as a doorstop."

It's a family business now, the picket line. Eleven Plumbrooks walked the Green in aprons Tuesday under a sign reading FIRST HELPING IS NOT A WAGE. At noon the Feastwarden's own mother crossed the grass with a basket of scones for the strikers. She didn't bring him one.

"Thirty years I've scrubbed pots for that family," said Hobb Tealeaf, a dishwasher and the only guild member who isn't related to anybody. "Never seen Sunday dinner this tense. And it's Tuesday."

Prudence Haverwick of Saltmarrow Banquets offered to cater the whole feast herself at her usual rate, which works out to roughly sixty-six thousand gold. Plumbrook called this "generous" and put it in his hat.

The committee meets tonight at the Sleeping Mule. The cooks plan to sit outside the door in chairs, on their lunch break. They've told the committee the break runs until Thursday.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Party Spends 1,000 gp on Heroes' Feast; Dragon Was Out
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: An adventuring party spent its whole 1,040 gp haul on a catered Heroes' Feast before a dragon fight. The dragon was out. Sterling sees a pivot.
item.content:encoded:
An adventuring party called the Brightmantle Company spent 1,000 gp of its 1,040 gp dungeon haul on a catered Heroes' Feast on Friday night, then marched into a young green dragon's lair in the Thornwood on Saturday morning to find the dragon not at home. The table came from Saltmarrow Banquets of Brindlemoor, which prices every Heroes' Feast at exactly the cost of the spell's jeweled bowl and sold out all thirty tables this month. I'll say it up front: this is the best consumer story of the season.

Look at the product. One hour of dinner, served by a cleric in a clean apron, and you walk away immune to poison and fear, with extra hit points and advantage on Wisdom saves for a full day. Against a green dragon, whose whole pitch is poison breath, that is perfect product-market fit. Saltmarrow's owner, Prudence Haverwick, told me the bowl gets consumed by the spell, so the customer pays for the bowl and the cleric, and she keeps the tip. "Think of us as the pre-boss experience," she said. I wrote that on my wrist.

The Brightmantles ate at sundown at a camp a mile from the lair. Their fighter, Corwin Dask, had three helpings of venison and announced he could "feel his hit points." The wizard slept in her robe so she wouldn't waste the morning dressing. At first light they kicked in the lair door and found a note nailed to the inside, in neat green ink: OUT AT DINNER. BACK SUNDAY. HELP YOURSELF TO THE MOSS.

The dragon, a young green named Verdigrass, had booked table nineteen at Saltmarrow Banquets for Saturday evening. Same caterer. Same bowl. Same 1,000 gp. Prudence Haverwick confirmed the reservation and called the dragon "a wonderful repeat customer who tips in emeralds." My accountant calls that a conflict of interest. I call that serving both sides of the market, which is what every great guild does sooner or later.

The party waited in the lair for nineteen hours, fully buffed and immune to poison, playing cards on a pile of moss. The feast wore off at sundown Saturday. Verdigrass came home Sunday morning, also immune to poison and fear, with extra hit points, and in an excellent mood. The Brightmantles left through a window with 40 gp, one card deck, and no rogue, who has since rightsized himself out of the adventuring party to join Saltmarrow's front-of-house staff. He gets the tips now. I call that a pivot.

Brakka Stonesweat will no doubt write that the party got fleeced by a caterer. Brakka once called a Heroes' Feast seating bid "a dinner with a velvet rope," so consider the source. When I met Guildmaster Tobrin Ashgrove at a balloon launch, he told me, "Sterling, never fight on an empty stomach, and never fight on a full one either." I still don't know what he meant. I think about it constantly.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:
- Buffs last 24 hours. Calendars last longer. Check the boss's.
- If your caterer knows the dragon's table number, ask what the dragon is having.
- Leave the rogue at home. He's networking.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Wizard Sells Prestidigitation Seasoning; Flavor Lasts 1 Hour
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: A party wizard sold Prestidigitation seasoning for trail rations at 2 cp a meal. The flavor lasts one hour. Lunch came at hour three. I subscribed anyway.
item.content:encoded:
Okay. OKAY. I just got back from nine days on the road with the Bramblegate Irregulars, and their wizard, Tamsin Quillowby, has launched a Prestidigitation seasoning service for trail rations. Two copper a meal and she flavors your hardtack with cinnamon, roast beef, or her premium blend, feast-day gravy. The one catch, which is in the spell and also in the fine print: the flavor lasts one hour.

I signed up on day one. Of course I did! A cantrip-based flavor layer on top of legacy biscuit hardware? The mana throughput on this thing is basically zero. Tamsin can cast it all day for free, which she mentioned to nobody while collecting copper from five people.

Day one was incredible. She seasoned breakfast at dawn and my hardtack tasted like a cinnamon bun that had been to a nice school. Then the party marched. The ranger wanted to reach the ford before dark, so we didn't stop to eat until three hours later, and by then the seasoning had expired. Lunch tasted like a roof tile. I filed a ticket. Tamsin said the service "is delivered at the time of casting" and that eating it later was "a user-side latency issue."

By day two, meals ran on Tamsin's schedule. Seasoning windows opened at dawn, noon, and dusk, and if you weren't chewing within the hour, too bad. We ate lunch at a dead run once. The cleric tried to save half a roast-beef biscuit for later and watched it slowly turn back into a biscuit, which she described to me as "the saddest thing I have seen, and I work funerals."

The real bottleneck was capacity. Tamsin can only keep three of these flavors going at once, and five of us were paying. So she rolled out a queue. Priority went to whoever paid for the week up front. I paid for the week up front. I would do it again, and that worries me.

Garrick, the party fighter, cancelled on day three over the 2 cp, on principle. He ate plain hardtack for the remaining six days while the rest of us sat around the fire going "mmm, gravy." On day five Tamsin offered him a free trial meal. He said no. On day six she cast roast beef on the air near his head, which she called "ambient marketing," and he threw his boot in the river.

This is how it always goes, isn't it? Remember the paladin who rented her Find Steed out to her own party? Same business model, different animal. I hate subscription fees. I also had gravy-flavored hardtack in a swamp on day eight and it was the happiest I have been all month.

Byte, my pseudodragon, has started saying "Flavor that fits your schedule! Your wizard's schedule!" at random intervals, so somebody's been feeding him the brochure. Brother Tumbleberry will tell you to just put salt on it. I think Brother Tumbleberry has never been offered gravy by a spell.

Rating: four out of five beholder eyes. Damage Report: copper spent, 54. Meals eaten at a run: 3. Boots lost to the river: 1 (Garrick's). Taste buds: confused but loyal.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

item.title: Gricks Eat Party's Feast Dinner in Room Nobody Searched
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: Four gricks got into an adventuring party's feast-week dinner in a dungeon room nobody had searched. One was in the stew. The cook is billing for the lid.
item.content:encoded:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 3, SIDE ROOM C — Gricks got into the Larkfallow Company's feast-week dinner last night, about forty feet under Brindlemoor. The adventuring party had made camp for a long rest in a room it hadn't searched, stacked the food sacks against the back wall and hung a ham over the cook-pot. By the time the stew was ready, three gricks were in the sacks and a fourth was in the pot.

The party had planned this supper for a tenday. Brindlemoor's Grand Feast is three days off, and the Larkfallows, booked below until the end of the month, wanted a feast week of their own: a smoked ham, two loaves of honey bread, a wheel of cheese and a pot of mutton stew. The room was dry. The floor was flat and the fire drew well. "We were going to search it after dinner," said the party's fighter, Odric Vane. "Dinner first. It was a feast."

Mabry Tollen, the hired cook, found the first one. She lifted the lid to stir and the stew stirred back. A grick is a worm about as long as a grown man, with four tentacles around a beak where its face ought to be, and this one had climbed into the warm pot and eaten most of the mutton. She hit it with the lid. "I've cooked in eleven dungeons," she told me. "You check the room. You check the room before anybody unpacks the onions."

The other three came out of the food sacks: one from the flour, one from the bread, and one from the cheese, which by the rogue's account it had no plans to leave. The fight went four rounds. Final box score: Vane at 14 hit points, the wizard at 6, the rogue at 11, and the cleric at full and apologizing. Tollen took no damage and has billed the party for a new lid.

The cleric had cast purify food and drink over the whole supper an hour before, as she does every feast week. The spell worked. "The stew was perfectly clean," she said. "There was a grick in it." The party's bard, who asked to be named, called the evening "a learning meal."

The ham survived, mostly. It hung from a ceiling hook out of reach, though one grick tried for it from the top of the bread sack for some time. The party ate the ham standing up and finished searching the room at midnight. They found two more gricks and a crack in the north wall they have agreed not to look into.

The Shieldwall Mutual Assurance Society, which insures the party, covers lost provisions only when camp was made "in a cleared area." The clerk at the Shieldwall Mutual counter asked me whether the room had been cleared. I said it had been cleared of dinner. She wrote that down.

I prodded the last sack with a ten-foot pole on my way out. The cheese kept the pole, and the grick inside it kept the cheese. That is my fifteenth ten-foot pole of the season. Tollen wants a clause about unsearched rooms in her next contract, and she has my support. I had been promised a slice of the honey bread. I rolled poorly.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Water Elemental Floods Cranberry Bogs; Sauce Hits 4 sp a Jar
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: A water elemental hired to flood the cranberry bogs won't leave, and sauce went from 5 cp to 4 sp a jar. The Grand Feast needs 250 jars. I did the sums.
item.content:encoded:
Cranberry sauce in Brindlemoor rose from 5 copper pieces a jar to 4 silver on Monday, an eightfold jump, after a water elemental hired to flood the Redwater Bogs for the harvest declined to go home. The Grand Feast on the Town Green is on the 26th, three days from now. (For anyone just joining us: Feastwarden Odo Plumbrook, a halfling, promised a feast for 2,000 on a 900 gp budget.)

First, some farming, because the sums depend on it. Cranberries are harvested wet. You flood the bog, knock the berries loose, and they float to the top, where you rake them into carts. Bog-keeper Tilly Marrowfen has done this with buckets and a sluice gate for thirty years. This autumn she paid a traveling wizard 15 gp to summon a water elemental instead, on the reasoning that it would take one afternoon.

It has taken four days. The elemental has raised the bogs to roughly twelve feet, ringed the floating berries in a slow red whirlpool, and drowns any rake that comes near. "It likes them," Marrowfen told me from the bank. "It keeps holding one up to the light." The wizard has left town. His invoice, she says, did not mention dismissal.

So supply went into the bog along with the rakes. Marrowfen normally sends Brindlemoor about 1,400 jars of sauce in the last week of harvest month. This week she has 61, bottled from berries that washed over the sluice gate. Demand did not fall at all, because everyone in town is coming to a feast. When the berries go down and the eaters stay put, the price goes up until enough people give up. At 4 sp, people are giving up.

Now to the Loaf Index, which is where I start to sweat. At 4.675 copper a loaf, one jar of sauce is 8.56 loaves. (I have checked this four times. I would like it to be fewer loaves.) The Feastwarden's plan calls for one jar per eight guests, which is 250 jars. Last week that was 12.5 gp. Today it is 100 gp, or 2,139 loaves, and there are only 61 jars to buy.

Plumbrook, speaking from a chair outside the Sleeping Mule Tavern, called the news "a strong start" and said the elemental "clearly understands what a good cranberry is." He then asked whether the feast could hire it to fill the punch bowls. I asked how the remaining budget stood after the 600 gp goose and the 591 gp egg. He said the budget was "in a very creative place."

My colleague Sterling Vanmoor wrote to say the market will sort itself out, and that he has bought six jars at 4 sp "before it really takes off." I would point out, gently, that a jar of sauce kept in a drawer does not go up in value. It goes up in mold.

My aunt Marigold put up eleven jars in the summer and is keeping them in the boot next to her savings. She has been offered 5 sp a jar by a neighbor and is holding out for six.

What this means for your pantry: if you own a jar, do not open it before Thursday. If you own a bucket, Tilly Marrowfen is paying.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Party Drinks 6 Unidentified Potions to Skip the Identify Fee
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: Friends, the Pinchpenny Company drank six unidentified potions to save 150 gold on an Identify spell. My clinic bill came to 610. Soup is on the house.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, the Pinchpenny Company came home from the Undermaw on Friday with six unidentified potions and a sage's quote of 150 gold to cast Identify on the lot. They drank all six that night instead, to save the fee. My clinic spent Saturday sorting out the results, and the bill came to 610 gold.

I'll start with the good news: everyone is alive. Now the rest. Their fighter, a large and cheerful woman named Brisa Holloway, is invisible. She walked into my clinic at dawn, or rather the door opened by itself and a voice said "sorry about this." Their cleric floats about four feet off the ground and has to be tied to a bedpost like a festival balloon. Their ranger now speaks only to animals. He had a long, earnest talk with my cat about the whole evening, and my cat has not looked at me the same way since.

Then there is the wizard, Tobin Reedle. The sixth vial was oil of slipperiness. You are meant to rub it on your boots, friends, not drink it. He has slid off every bench in the building, two cots, and one visiting priest. His spoon will not stay in his hand, so we feed him broth through a reed.

"We did the arithmetic," Brisa told me from somewhere near the window. "Twenty-five gold a vial is robbery. Drinking them is free." I gently pointed out that my clinic is not free, and that I had also done the arithmetic.

The old herbals have a line about this: never taste what you cannot name. The Brindlemoor Alchemists' Circle went further last spring and tallied 340 delvers who drank unknown vials. Fewer than half got anything useful, and one in nine needed a priest by sundown. I know these numbers by heart. You would be amazed how often I recite them to people lying on my floor.

This is the third party this month. The Fourth Attempt drank nine unidentified potions on the first, and the Brass Kettle Company went through eleven to find the healing one, which was naturally the last. I am starting to think the Undermaw leaves them out as bait.

So, gently, here is the arithmetic. Identify: 150 gold, done by teatime, and nobody floats. My clinic: 610 gold, one ruined ceiling, and a cat with opinions. The sage is cheaper, friends. The sage is always cheaper. My friend Nyx tells me someone is selling a gadget that names a potion from a sketch of the bottle. Go outside, Nyx.

The invisible fighter should wear a bell until it wears off, which the clinic expects by Tuesday. The floating cleric should stay tethered. For all of them, I prescribe a pot of potato-and-leek, eaten slowly, with both feet on the floor if you can manage it.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: Kobolds Take 120 Feast Pies, Leave Thank-You Notes
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: Kobolds took 120 pies cooling on Brindlemoor windowsills for the Grand Feast. They thought the pies were offerings, and left thank-you notes. Allegedly.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell after midnight on Sunday, 120 pies cooling on Brindlemoor windowsills for the Grand Feast allegedly vanished, and the thieves were kobolds. A small warren under Tanner's Row thought the pies were offerings, carried off every one, and left a thank-you note on each sill.

The pies were the feast committee's cheapest plan yet. The committee has 900 gp and has promised to feed 2,000 people on the Town Green on the 26th, so Feastwarden Odo Plumbrook asked forty households to bake three pies each and set them out to cool. All forty did, which Plumbrook calls the best turnout of the season.

The notes are in charcoal, in Common, mostly. "THANK YOU FOR PIE," reads the one left for Marigold Tench, who was standing in her nightgown holding a rolling pin when I got there. "WE ARE VERY HONORED. THE APPLE ONE WAS BEST. WE LEFT YOU A GOOD TRAP." The good trap was a thread across the sill tied to a bell, and it drops a paper flower on anyone who reaches for the missing pie. "It got me twice," said Tench. "The flower's quite nice, honestly."

I'm a kobold myself, so let me explain. In a warren, anything left up high at night, still warm, is for the dragon. If no dragon turns up, it's allegedly for whoever got there first. Forty sills of warm pies in a row is the biggest offering any kobold has ever seen. They allegedly carried them home in a line, one pie per kobold, with a lookout at the front. One kobold's only job was to sing.

The warren calls itself the Clatterhole. It lives under an old cooperage behind a door the size of a breadbox. I found it by following crumbs and one dropped cherry. Ozzle Pinchwick, who speaks for the Clatterhole and was wearing a pie tin as a hat at the time, came out to talk. "We thought the town finally liked us," Pinchwick said. "One hundred and twenty pies! We voted on whether we deserved them. We decided yes."

Pinchwick then showed me a pit trap dug just for my foot and asked me to step in it, for fun. I did. It was an inch deep and had a cushion in it. The pie tin, by the way, was polished so bright you could see the moon in it. Anyway.

Plumbrook took the news standing on a chair at the Sleeping Mule. "This is a strong start," he said. "Our pies are so good a whole warren thought they were sacred. You can't buy a review like that." Asked where 120 new pies come from with four days to go, he said the Clatterhole had offered to help, that he had said yes, and that he did not yet know what he had said yes to. The giant crab in the East Gate is also still there.

Pinchwick says every pie tin will come back washed, and that the warren has started "a surprise for the feast, with springs in it." The City Watch was allegedly told about the surprise and asked how big the springs were. Pinchwick held two claws about this far apart. The Watch went home.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Wizard's Arcane Lock Seals Council Out; Nobody Wrote Password
item.dc:creator: Ottoline Vex
item.description: A hired adventuring party's wizard cast Arcane Lock on Brindlemoor's council chamber, and nobody wrote the password down. Council now meets in the snow.
item.content:encoded:
Brindlemoor's Burgess Council held its latest session on the front steps of its own chamber, in the snow, after the wizard of a hired adventuring party cast Arcane Lock on the doors and nobody wrote down the password. The wizard, Quenby Marrowind of the Fairlatch Company, maintains the password was "something about a goat."

The Council engaged the Fairlatch Company, four adventurers at 12 silver the night, to secure the chamber after last month's business with the ballot box that ate 31 votes. The contract asks the party to "make the chamber secure." It does not ask them to make it openable afterward. I have read the contract twice, and so has the Clerk. It is a very good contract. Nobody read it before signing.

For readers who skipped civic magic, Arcane Lock holds a door shut for as long as the caster likes and lets through anyone who speaks the password. The caster chooses the password. The caster is then expected to remember it. Mr. Marrowind chose his at about two in the morning, after the party's rogue bet him a silver he couldn't make it rhyme.

Debate opened on the third step at nine. Councilor Maldrith Quennel, the gentleman from the Chandler Ward, who is a lich and asks for everything in writing, moved that the party produce the password in writing. The motion was seconded. The party's fighter, a large woman named Brannagh Tusk, replied, "That's the whole problem, sir." Quennel, being dead, was untroubled by the snow. The other eight Burgesses were troubled by it and said so at length.

After ninety minutes of procedure, the Council voted to allow the party three guesses an hour. The minutes, kept on the Clerk's sleeve because the minute book is inside, record the following attempts: "goat," "goats," "the goat," "billy," "a goat is fine," and, from the rogue, "open up, it's us." The doors refused each one. The party's halfling cleric then tried "something about a goat," word for word. The doors refused that too, which Mr. Marrowind called "a relief, honestly."

Brindlemoor has one licensed caster of Knock, who is in Ashenfold for her sister's wedding until Tuesday. Reeve Maudrey Fennick of Brindlemoor told reporters, "We are aware of the door." She confirmed that an axe was discussed and ruled out, because the doors are listed with the Heritage Committee, and the Heritage Committee meets inside.

By my count the session produced six Promises Made, including "we'll be in by lunch," and one Promise Kept: a motion to hold the next session on the steps as well, which passed 9-0 because nobody could reach the rulebook to object. A courtier who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to be awake suggested the password may involve the goat from last week's rally. Mr. Marrowind said he had attended that rally, then went quiet for some time.

The Fairlatch Company has offered the Council a full refund of 12 silver. Quennel has asked for the offer in writing. The quills are inside.

— O.V., from the gallery

item.title: Party's Earth Elemental Clears Snow, Cobbles and Half a Wall
item.dc:creator: Brakka Stonesweat
item.description: A broke adventuring party underbid the shovellers and sent an earth elemental to clear the snow. It took the cobbles too. Now there's a picket line.
item.content:encoded:
The earth elemental got the snow. It got the street too.

An adventuring party short on winter coin took a snow-clearing contract in Brindlemoor on Thursday and had its druid conjure an earth elemental to do the digging. The elemental cleared the snow on Tanner's Row. It then cleared 187 cobblestones, a garden fence and half a cooper's wall, and the Brindlemoor Shovellers' Lodge has picketed the party's tavern ever since.

The party calls itself the Lean Winter Company. Four adventurers. By their own count they had 9 silver between them, since the Undermaw goes quiet for the season and the monsters stop paying. The ward clerk posted the job at 30 silver for three streets. The Lodge bid 45, which buys 31 shovellers, a dawn start and a hot lunch. The Lean Winter bid 12. That means they undercut a union with a spell.

"I have dug that street for twenty-two winters," said Ulla Coldmitten, a snow-shoveller and the Lodge's steward. "You learn where the cobbles are. You go around them. That's the whole trade. The rock fellow did not go around them."

The druid, Bryony Thatchwell, says the first hour went beautifully. The elemental moved through the drifts "like a mole through custard." Then she sneezed. After that, she said, it "got very enthusiastic about the job." It worked down to the clay. It put the fence somewhere. Nobody has found the fence.

Hal Brennick, a cooper, came outside to find half his wall gone and his barrels looking at the street. "I asked it to stop," he said. "It looked at me like I was more snow."

The clerk paid the company its 12 silver on Friday. He also sent a bill for the cobbles: 40 gold. In plain speech, the job cost them about 40 gold and paid them a tip.

The picket stands outside The Sleeping Mule Tavern, where the company rents two rooms. Thirty-one shovellers walk it, shovels on shoulders, singing a song about fences that I won't print. The Mule's landlady reports business is up, because picketers drink. The company has eaten every meal upstairs. "We had a druid. They had shovels. It seemed like math," said Dorran Pike, the company's fighter, through a window. "I'm learning the math was wrong."

The Lodge wants the contract back, an apology in writing, and the Lean Winter on the line with real shovels at Lodge rates, with a proper lunch break. Thatchwell has agreed to the lunch. Talks continue.

"Nobody here is against magic," Coldmitten said. "I'm against magic that works for 12 silver and doesn't know what a fence is."

I've got nothing against broke adventurers. I've been broke. But undercut the folk who live off a job and next winter the clerk remembers the 12. Not the 45. Even the frost giant clearing the Rimeback Pass asked for a proper wage.

Solidarity. And stretch your back. — Brakka

item.title: Paladin's Find Steed Ride-Share Vanishes Mid-River Over 1 Star
item.dc:creator: Nyx Spindlecoil
item.description: A paladin rented her Find Steed warhorse to her own party at 3 sp a head, then dismissed it mid-ford over a one-star rating. Nyx was aboard.
item.content:encoded:
Ser Wynna Brackenridge, paladin of the Thistledown Oath, cast Find Steed on Tuesday morning and rented the warhorse to her own adventuring party as a ride-share, 3 silver a head, from Brindlemoor to Ashenfold. Halfway across the Millrace ford, the party's wizard rated the ride one star. Ser Wynna dismissed the steed as an action, the horse disappeared, and its passengers fell into the river. I was one of them!

Okay. OKAY. Before the river, let me tell you about the launch, because the launch was beautiful. Ser Wynna calls the service Steedshare, and the pitch is gorgeous: one 10-minute cast, a celestial warhorse with an Intelligence of 6, and no hay, no stable fees, no subscription. NO SUBSCRIPTION. Do you know how long I have waited for a mount without a monthly plan? She even offered telepathic route updates to the driver within a mile. Runic latency: zero. Mana throughput: one 2nd-level slot, unlimited miles.

The seating chart was aggressive. Orrin Pegwhistle, the wizard, rode up front. Dabble Fenn, the rogue, sat behind him. I was wedged on the saddlebags with my familiar Byte on my head. Ser Wynna walked alongside holding the fare ledger, because, as she put it, "the driver's seat was the most profitable seat, so I sold it." That made four riders on one warhorse, if you count Byte, which Byte insists you do.

Steedshare also has ratings. Riders score each trip from one to five stars, and the score goes straight to the driver. Orrin's score came in at the deepest part of the ford. He cited "the trot" and "a faint smell of sulfur," which is fair, since Ser Wynna had picked fiend as the steed's type. She told me fiend was the only option with heated seats.

"The spell is very clear," Ser Wynna said afterward, wringing out her tabard. "I may dismiss my steed at any time as an action. I took that action." Orrin, still in the water, said he would give the river two stars.

Recasting the spell would have summoned the same horse at full hit points, which is a lovely feature! Ser Wynna had no 2nd-level slots left, though, having spent her last one that morning smiting a goose that hissed at the Steedshare banner. So we walked the last nine miles to Ashenfold. At the gate she charged each of us a 1 sp cancellation fee, because the ride had technically been cancelled by the driver.

I already know Brother Tumbleberry will write that this proves we should all walk and touch grass. Wendell, I touched riverweed. That counts. This is also the second time this month a ride-hire service has billed me for its own disaster, after the carpet of flying surge pricing mess, and I will keep riding them all.

Byte surfaced, spat out a minnow, and said, "Your journey, your way." Four out of five beholder eyes. A celestial warhorse for 3 silver is a miracle, right up until somebody rates it.

Damage Report: Passengers dunked: 3, plus one pseudodragon. Stars given: 1. Cancellation fees paid: 3 sp. Eyebrows: wet, but present.

— Nyx (they/them). Damage Report below.

item.title: Giant Crab for Feast Wedged in Brindlemoor Town Gate
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: The Fourth Attempt brought a giant crab home for the Grand Feast. It is 14 feet across, the East Gate is 10, and the crab is now stuck halfway through.
item.content:encoded:
THE EAST GATE, BRINDLEMOOR, STREET LEVEL, HALFWAY UNDER A CRAB — The Fourth Attempt came home Friday night with a new centerpiece for the Grand Feast: one giant crab, fourteen feet from claw to claw, caught in the tide pools below Kelpmouth. The East Gate is ten feet wide. As of this morning the crab is stuck in it, about halfway, and the adventuring party that caught it is on the wrong side of it.

For anyone just arriving: Feastwarden Odo Plumbrook promised a feast for 2,000 on the Town Green on the 26th, on 900 gp. The first centerpiece, Duchess, gave birth to nine piglets on Thursday, and the town will not hear of eating her. Plumbrook had a new job notice up by Friday breakfast. The Fourth Attempt, who brought Duchess in, took it for 40 gp and caught the morning barge.

Ansel Pottage, steward of the party's hirelings, read me the clause by lantern light. "Bring back one (1) centerpiece fit to feed two thousand, to the Town Green, by Saturday." He folded the paper. "I measured the crab. Nobody asked me to measure the gate. Nobody ever does."

The trouble is the walk. A crab goes sideways, which brings the widest part of it to the gate first. The fighter tried four times to turn it face-on, and four times it turned back. Then the wizard cast Enlarge/Reduce, the crab shrank to the size of a cart, and the party hurried it under the arch. That spell lasts only as long as the wizard keeps her mind on it. Halfway through, the crab pinched the rogue, the wizard looked round, and the crab came back to full size with its shell jammed against both gateposts.

Box score at the gate: fighter 14 hit points (of 38), rogue 6 (of 24), wizard 22 (of 22), crab at full health and dug in. I lost my fourteenth ten-foot pole of the season trying to lever a claw off the left post. The pole is in two pieces now. I rolled poorly on that.

Gatekeeper Oswin Hask, who has kept the East Gate for nineteen years, has closed it to carts. "I've had a hay wagon stuck in this gate, and once an ogre," he said. "Neither one pinched." The fish carts are going round by the North Gate, an hour out of their way. Hask is charging the crab the livestock toll of two copper a leg, and he counts ten legs.

Plumbrook spoke from a chair on the town side. "A strong start," he said. "Our centerpiece is already halfway to the Green." Asked how one crab feeds 2,000, he said it was "a very big crab" and that the committee was "looking into butter." Keeper Bess Harrowgate sent word from the Sleeping Mule that she has no stall that size and would want a deposit. The party's bard, who asked to be named, says the crab "chose us."

The wizard is resting and will try again at dawn. Chapter 9 has offered the loan of a crowbar at five silver an hour. Five days remain. By noon, a boy from Fish Street had started calling the crab the Admiral, and I have asked him to stop. Hilde Brackwater has already been by with a blanket.

— H.D., filing from below

item.title: Giant Eagles Refuse Party's Escort Plan: 'Not a Coach Service'
item.dc:creator: Grashka Ironjaw
item.description: The Updraft Company planned its whole escort job around riding giant eagles over the pass. Nobody asked the eagles. The eagles said no. Twelve siege-days.
item.content:encoded:
The adventuring party hired to escort Duke Osgar Wendmoor of Varnholt to Brindlemoor's Grand Feast built its entire plan around giant eagles. On Thirdday the giant eagles of the Talonspire said no. The Updraft Company had never asked them. Tension holds at twelve siege-days.

The contract paid 900 gold to get the duke, eleven courtiers, and nineteen trunks across the Rimeback Pass, which is shut by snow and, last I checked, by a frost giant arguing about his wages. The party's wizard drew the plan on the back of the contract. Walk to the Talonspire. Whistle. Fly. That was the whole plan. I have seen it. It has a drawing of a bird.

"Eagles show up," said Bryn Ostley, who leads the Updraft Company and named it after the plan. "That's what eagles do. Everyone knows the eagles show up."

They did not show up. The party climbed the Talonspire instead and asked for a parley on the top ledge. Skyreeve Aethra, eldest of the roost, came out to meet them. The talon-shake lasted two seconds. Firm. No hidden dagger detected. One hidden mouse, which she ate.

"We are not a coach service," the Skyreeve said. "We have eggs. We have a winter. Did you write ahead?" They had not. She asked if the duke knew her name. The duke, who had come up the cliff in a litter carried by four courtiers, called her "the big one." Tension climbed four siege-days in one sentence. I have seen border wars start slower.

The duke's chamberlain offered gold. Eagles carry no purses and said so. He offered fish, and the roost counted the fish twice and came back with a counteroffer of more fish. Then a courtier opened trunk number seven to prove its contents were light. It was shoes. Forty pairs. The trunk outweighs the party's cleric. Aethra said the eagles fly for causes, and footwear is not a cause. The parley ended there.

The delegation is now walking. The pass is forty miles of snow, the courtiers wear silk slippers, and the Feast is in nine days. The party handed out field rations at the bottom of the cliff. The duke refused his hardtack. I ate it. Excellent hardtack. Dense. Honest. It does not need to be flown anywhere.

Ottoline Vex covered the same parley from a heated tent at the foot of the Talonspire and called it "a frank exchange between partners." It was frank. I was on the ledge. An eagle took my hat, and she got a cup of mulled cider.

Ostley says the party has moved to Plan B. I asked to see Plan B. It is the same drawing with a second bird. The eagles have not been asked about that one either.

Ironjaw, filed from the front.

item.title: Yeti Fur Coats Up 300% After First Snow; Yetis Unimpressed
item.dc:creator: Barnaby Tallowmere
item.description: Brindlemoor's first snow sent yeti fur coats from 45 gp to 180 gp in two days. The yetis came down from the pass to say they are still wearing theirs.
item.content:encoded:
Yeti fur coats rose 300% in Brindlemoor this week, from 45 gp to 180 gp, after the town's first snow fell on Tuesday night. By Thursday the yetis of the Rimeback Pass had walked down to the toll house to say, through a very patient interpreter, that they are still wearing all of their fur and would like to know whose coats these are.

Let me put the price in plain terms. At 4 copper a loaf, the old coat was 1,125 loaves. The new coat is 4,500 loaves. (I have checked this four times. I checked it a fifth time out of pure dread.) A family of four could eat bread for three years on one sleeve.

The rise started at Fernsley's Outfitters, where Hobb Fernsley chalked the new price on his window before the snow had finished settling. "Demand is up," he told me, warming his hands on the cash box. "Cold weather is foot traffic for the shoulders." By Wednesday the coats had sold out, so Fernsley started selling paper. A "pelt note" is a slip promising one yeti fur coat "upon delivery of yeti." Notes changed hands on the bench outside his shop at 60 gp, then 90, then 140, among people who own no coat and in several cases no yeti.

Somebody should explain the economics, so I will. When a price rises because people expect to resell at a higher price, rather than because anyone needs more warmth, it is a bubble. It holds as long as the next buyer believes. One speculator, a cooper named Dunstan Rook, holds 31 notes and could not tell me what color a yeti is. "White," he guessed. "Or brown. It goes up either way."

Then Grandmother Hulda Whitebrow arrived. She is the eldest of the Rimeback's yetis, about nine feet tall, and she smelled of pine and old snow. In Fernsley's doorway she rubbed a display coat between two enormous fingers and said it was goat. Her grandson translated the rest: yetis shed in spring, not when merchants feel chilly, and the clan has not sold a single hair to anyone in living memory. "We are using it," she said. "It is snowing."

Fernsley pointed out that his tag reads "Yeti-Style Fur." The fine print says "yeti" refers to the cut. Note prices fell to 12 gp by sundown. Rook paid an average of 90 gp a note, so he is down 2,418 gp, or 60,450 loaves. He is a cooper, at least, so he has a barrel to live in.

My colleague Sterling Vanmoor called the episode "a healthy outerwear moment" and bought four notes at the top. My aunt Marigold keeps her savings in a boot, and the boot is lined with an honest wool sock that has never pretended to be anything else. I have never respected a sock more.

What this means for your pantry: buy flour, buy a goat-fur coat at goat-fur prices, and do not buy a promise of a yeti from a man on a bench.

— B.T. (Loaf Index: see sidebar)

item.title: Feast Boar Has 9 Piglets; Town Won't Eat a New Mother
item.dc:creator: Brother Wendell Tumbleberry
item.description: Duchess, the giant boar meant to headline Brindlemoor's Grand Feast, had 9 piglets six days out. No one will eat a new mother. Brother Wendell says soup.
item.content:encoded:
Friends, Duchess, the giant boar brought in from the Thornwood to be the centerpiece of Brindlemoor's Grand Feast, gave birth to nine piglets in the big stall at the Sleeping Mule late Thursday night. The feast is on the Town Green on the 26th, six days from now, and as of this morning not one soul in town will agree to eat a new mother.

For anyone just joining us: Feastwarden Odo Plumbrook promised a feast for 2,000 on a 900 gp budget, and Duchess was the plan for the middle of the table. Everyone called her a boar. That is what happens when you let the hunters who caught her decide such things. Nobody checked, and Duchess did not volunteer it.

Keeper Bess Harrowgate, who rents Duchess the stall, found the litter at the late bell. "Nine of them, and every one hungry," she said. "House rule six is no eating the guests. Last night we had one guest in that stall. This morning I count ten." She has opened a second page in the ledger and written "piglets, nine, minors" at the top.

Plumbrook gave his statement standing on a chair outside the stable door. "This is a strong start," he said. "We wanted a centerpiece. Now we have a centerpiece with nine smaller centerpieces." Asked what 2,000 people will eat on the 26th, he said the committee was "exploring the menu" and climbed down. Mortimer, the tavern's mule, brayed from the woodshed for the length of the speech and some while after.

Brindlemoor has taken her side. A petition reading LEAVE DUCHESS BE had 640 marks by noon, three of them from the butchers' guild. Hilde Brackwater, a turnip farmer, brought a blanket and a basket and stood by the stall door to shoo off gawkers. A little girl from Fish Street has named the runt Turnip, so that is settled too.

Now, the health part. The old herbals say a sow with a new litter wants to be kept warm and fed a great deal, and left unfussed for a full moon. The Midwives' Hall ran a study on farm sows last spring and found that a mother nursing a big litter eats close to twice her usual feed. Duchess already ate two bushels of turnips a day. Harrowgate tells me the lease did not foresee four. Please don't crowd the stall, friends. She has tusks, and she has had a long night.

My friend Nyx Spindlecoil sent word that she could hang a scrying mirror over the straw so the whole realm can watch the piglets sleep. Go outside, Nyx. Walk over and look at them quietly, like a person.

As for the feast, I have a suggestion nobody on the committee asked for. Turnip-and-barley soup, made in the biggest pot in Brindlemoor, feeds two thousand for about 40 gold, and nobody has to look a mother in the eye. Duchess has eaten most of the town's turnips, so do buy them early.

Rest well, friends. — Brother Wendell

item.title: 'Unlimited' Tiny Hut Is 10 Feet Wide. Six Heroes, One Mule Tried
item.dc:creator: Sterling Vanmoor
item.description: Voidpocket Labs sold a party an 'unlimited' Tiny Hut for a winter long rest. The fine print says 10 feet across. They were six plus a mule. I see density.
item.content:encoded:
A party of six adventurers and one mule spent Tuesday night inside a single boxed Tiny Hut on the Frostgate Road, after Voidpocket Labs sold them its new Hut-in-a-Box Unlimited for 75 gp. The fine print, printed on the inside of the lid, puts the dome at 10 feet across. Nobody in the party got a long rest. I have rarely been more excited about a product.

The party calls itself the Ironkettle Company. They bought the hut for the winter road north of Brindlemoor, where snow and owlbears make an open camp a bad idea. The box says UNLIMITED in gold leaf on all four sides. Below that, in letters a halfling would squint at, it says "unlimited uses per tenday, dome 10 ft. across, occupancy subject to geometry." The packaging calls the floor plan "cozy-first." Synergy, friends. Voidpocket already did this once with its unlimited Endless Sack, and I bought two of those.

"We read 'unlimited' and figured it meant room," said Tamsin Oakhollow, the party's ranger, who spent the night with the mule's tail across her face. "It meant we could be miserable as often as we liked." The fighter slept standing up in his plate, because the plate would not fit on the floor. The wizard's spellbook went under the dwarf. The chest of 2,000 copper went under the wizard. The mule, a gray named Biscuit, took the middle and kicked whoever got close, which was everyone.

Here is what the haters miss. Voidpocket did not sell a cramped hut. Voidpocket sold a co-resting space with zero wasted square footage. Six adventurers, one mule, and a fortune in copper, all inside the same warm dome while a blizzard howled outside. That is density. That is a lean camp. That party woke up closer than any party in the realm, and the cleric is not speaking to the bard, which I'd call a natural rightsizing of the adventuring party.

Voidpocket representative Odalys Brindlefoot told me by sending stone that the hut "performed exactly as described on the lid," and that a Family Dome, 20 feet across, is available as a 40 gp upgrade. The Ironkettles asked for a refund. She offered them a second hut. They set the two side by side and learned the domes do not connect. The mule picked one. The party took the other.

Brakka Stonesweat will write that this is a scam on working adventurers. Brakka has never scaled anything but a tavern stair. I once shared a carriage with Guildmaster Pellam Strood of the Lanternwright Consortium, and he told me, "Sterling, the customer always wants more room. Sell them the feeling of room." I think about that every time I fold myself into my own Hut-in-a-Box, which is nightly, for the discipline.

Key takeaways for the ambitious adventurer:

- Read the lid before you trust the box.
- Every mule is a stakeholder.
- Small footprint, big upside.

— Sterling Vanmoor, Guild Visionary. Let's connect at the Yawning Portal.

item.title: Wizard's Gust of Wind Clears Market Leaves and 14 Stalls
item.dc:creator: Skritch Mudwhistle
item.description: A wizard offered to sweep the leaves off Brindlemoor's market square with Gust of Wind. The leaves left. So did 14 stalls and a pumpkin cart. Allegedly.
item.content:encoded:
At roughly the second bell after noon, a wizard from the Lanternmoth Company cast Gust of Wind down the length of Brindlemoor's market square to clear away the autumn leaves, and allegedly cleared away 14 market stalls, 6 awnings, and one full cart of pumpkins along with them. The leaves are gone. Nobody disputes that part.

The wizard, a halfling named Fennimore Pallthistle, says he was only being helpful. The square's sweeper had leaned his broom against the fishmonger's stall and gone for soup, and Pallthistle allegedly volunteered to "save everyone an afternoon." Witnesses say he did not look down the row first. He did not check who was standing in it. He pointed his hand toward the far end of the square and said the word.

"It was a beautiful line of wind," said Marta Greel, who was buying turnips at the time and is now buying them from a different stall, since hers is on a roof. "Very straight. Very long. I would call it about sixty feet of no more market."

Vendors report that the leaves went first, in a lovely gold swirl, and then the awnings went, and then the tables went, and then the pumpkins rolled the length of the square and into the horse trough at the end like a very orange avalanche. The cheese seller's sign was found three streets over. A rack of wool hats allegedly reached the Undermaw gate. Every pigeon on the square was blown clean over the chapel, which this reporter counts as the only good news of the week.

The worst part, according to the vendors, is that Pallthistle held the spell. Gust of Wind keeps blowing while the caster concentrates, and he allegedly kept concentrating for most of a minute because, in his words, "there were still some leaves by the well." There were. There are not now. There is also no well cover.

The rest of the Lanternmoth Company arrived halfway through. Their fighter, Bryn Tolloway, tried to grab the pumpkin cart and was blown into the trough with it. Their cleric is said to have watched the whole thing from the bakery steps holding a sticky bun and "declining to get involved." Speaking of which, there was a brass weathervane spinning on top of the bakery the whole time, and it is honestly the shiniest thing on the square. Anyway.

Watch Sergeant Adda Kemble of the City Watch arrived after the wind stopped and wrote the company up for 88 gold in damages, payable to the vendors. That is on top of what wizards around here already owe since the Rattlepan Company's Thunderwave took out a tavern wall two days ago. Market stall holders have now lost stalls twice this month, after the veterans parade kicked in 12 of them.

Pallthistle maintains the job was done. "They asked for no leaves," he said, standing in the empty square. "Look around. Do you see a single leaf?" This reporter looked around. He did not. He also did not see a market.

The sweeper has his broom back. It was allegedly found on the chapel roof with the pigeons.

— Skritch, on the beat (allegedly)

item.title: Carrion Crawler Takes Post After Party Evicts Skeleton Guards
item.dc:creator: Hollis Delvewright
item.description: An adventuring party wheeled six striking skeletons off Level 2 for 30 gp. Forty minutes later a carrion crawler had their post. Hit points tallied.
item.content:encoded:
THE UNDERMAW, LEVEL 2, 40 FEET DOWN — A carrion crawler moved into the empty skeleton guardpost on Level 2 this morning. Forty minutes earlier, the Gravelstep Five, an adventuring party hired by Chapter 9 to clear the level, had carried out the six skeletons who were sitting in it. The skeletons were on strike. The party had been told they were an obstruction.

The contract, which I have read all the way to the end, paid 30 gp to remove "undead obstructions from the Level 2 vault corridor." The six skeletons who walked off the post earlier this month were still on their picket, with their skull for a cup. They did not fight. "They went limp," said the party's fighter, Marta Quillon. "Have you ever carried a skeleton that's gone limp? It's all elbows." The Five took them up to the Level 1 landing in a wheelbarrow, two at a time, which is three trips.

Then they went back down for their voucher, and the box score went like this. The rogue stepped into the guardpost and was paralyzed at the door. The wizard, reaching for him, was paralyzed reaching. The fighter went in at 26 hit points and came out at 7, carrying the wizard. The rogue stayed where he was. The carrion crawler, eight feet of it, had curled up under the sergeant's old stool as if it had been issued the stool. The party's bard, who asked to be named, said, "In fairness, it is in exactly the spot they stood for four hundred years."

The skeleton sergeant came back down at noon to collect a boot he had left behind. He looked at the crawler, and at the party, and at the wheelbarrow. He then levered the crawler off the rogue with the butt of his spear, the way you would move a dog off a chair, and charged the Five 4 sp. "Relief shift," he said. "That is the rate."

Chapter 9 does not see a problem. Deputy Registrar Pell Oddingwick confirmed the post is occupied. "The vacancy has been filled," he said, adding that the Guild's maps list the post as manned, "which it now is." Asked whether the crawler is on the payroll, he said it had not asked to be. The Five have not been paid. Chapter 9's position is that the contract was to clear the corridor, and the corridor is not clear.

The skeletons are now in the back room of the Sleeping Mule, on credit. Keeper Bess Harrowgate says six tenants who do not eat is the best week she has had since the cube. Their claim for four centuries of back wages is still before Examiner Odalys Brackenmoor. The sergeant says they will not return to the post now. "It has a tenant," he said.

I lost another ten-foot pole prodding the stool. I rolled poorly on the stool. Chapter 9 still calls Level 2 mostly cleared, and mostly now has a crawler in it.

— H.D., filing from below
